edges.rationale: The major scale is a fixed pattern of the tones and semitones a student first measures on the keyboard.
The chromatic scale is every semitone in a row, so it is the semitone step repeated twelve times.
An interval number counts letter names including both ends, while semitones count keys; students call C to E a 2nd because there are two tones.
A sharp key signature is a set of sharps written once at the start instead of beside every note.
A flat key signature is a set of flats written once at the start instead of beside every note.
An accidental lasts only to the bar line, but a key signature lasts the whole piece; students carry one rule into the other.
Both cover double sharps and flats: pitch reads the signs, keys uses them to spell scale notes and enharmonics correctly.
Respelling a note enharmonically is how a double sharp or flat is named as an ordinary note.
Writing the chromatic scale means choosing between enharmonic spellings of each black key.
C to D sharp and C to E flat sound the same, yet one is an augmented 2nd and one a minor 3rd: interval names follow spelling, not sound.
Counting lines and spaces between two notes gives the interval number; a step is a 2nd and a skip a 3rd.
Reading by interval and finding an interval at the keyboard are the same distance judgement, one from the page and one to the keys.
A compound interval is a simple interval plus an octave, which only works because octaves share a letter name.
Rewriting a note in another clef at the same pitch and transposing it by an octave look alike on paper; students answer one when asked the other.
The groups of two and three black keys are the landmarks a hand finds for scales like B, D flat and F sharp major.
E sharp and B sharp occur in F sharp and C sharp major, and C flat and F flat in G flat and C flat major.
Starting any scale means finding its tonic key first.
The tonic triad lies under fingers 1, 3 and 5 of a five-finger position on the tonic.
A two-octave scale moves the hand into a new position with each thumb-under and finger-over.
An arpeggio spans more than a hand, so it is a chain of position shifts.
A root-position triad is three notes a skip apart, all on lines or all in spaces.
Naming the root, third and fifth means counting alternate letter names, as in C, E and G.
Which inversion a chord is in depends only on its lowest note, usually read in the bass staff.
A block triad on the tonic is fingers 1, 3 and 5 of a five-finger position played at once.
A beamed group takes one stem direction, set by the note furthest from the middle line.
Sight-reading a line means counting the rhythm while reading the pitches, not one after the other.
Left-hand rhythm practice reads from the bass staff, so slow bass reading breaks the pulse.
An accidental above or below an ornament sign alters the ornament's upper or lower note.
The viola reads the alto clef, so naming instruments' clefs relies on reading it.
Cello, bassoon and trombone read the tenor clef in high passages.
In a string quartet's open score the viola part is written in the alto clef.
Short score puts soprano and alto on the treble staff and tenor and bass on the bass staff of a grand staff.
The right hand's part is usually on the treble staff, so practising it alone is treble reading at the keyboard.
The left hand's part is usually on the bass staff, so practising it alone is bass reading at the keyboard.
Sight-reading a piece at one's level builds on sight-reading a single line in each hand.
Reading from landmark notes instead of counting up from the bottom line is a core sight-reading strategy.
Both nodes cover metronome marks: rhythm reads the beat unit and number, expression uses them to set the tempo.
Ties and slurs are both curves; a tie joins two of the same pitch into one held note, a slur asks for legato across different pitches.
Students re-strike a tied note as if it were slurred, or hold a slurred note as if it were tied.
Legato needs each note held for its full value until the next one sounds.
Staccato shortens a note against its written value, so the habit of holding values full fights it.
Playing at the marked tempo needs control of pulse at that speed, slow or fast.
Syncopation moves stress off the beat, and the accent sign is how that stress is usually marked.
Legato pedalling changes just after the beat, the same off-beat timing a syncopated rhythm uses.
Rit. and accel. deliberately move the pulse; a student trained to hold it steady resists them, or drifts where nothing is marked.
An acciaccatura takes almost no time while an appoggiatura takes half the main note's value, so reading them means knowing that value.
A tempo term and a metronome mark both say how fast, one in words and one in beats per minute.
Both cover the upbeat: rhythm counts it into the bar, pieces finds it at the start of phrases.
Coming in on an upbeat in a piece is the upbeat rhythm played with the piece's count-in.
Different rhythms in each hand are the hard case of keeping rhythm with hands together.
Practising the left hand alone is mostly keeping its rhythm steady without the melody to lean on.
Building a piece up to tempo means holding the pulse as the metronome rises.
Slow practice works when the student counts the subdivisions aloud instead of letting slow notes drift.
A piece's tempo marking often carries a metronome mark that sets the target speed.
A Roman numeral names a chord by the scale degree of its root.
A triad's quality is read the same way as an interval's: from the qualities of its third and fifth above the root.
Diminished and augmented triads are named for their diminished or augmented fifth.
The diminished fifth between the third and seventh of V7 is what pulls it to resolve inward.
The raised seventh of the harmonic minor makes V major and VII diminished in a minor key.
The melodic minor's raised sixth is for melody; students build minor-key chords from it instead of from the harmonic minor.
The minor key signature leaves out the raised leading note, so students play V as a minor chord.
IV and V are the keys on either side of I on the circle of fifths.
Figures like 6/3 and 6/4 are interval numbers above the bass.
Choosing chords for a melody starts from knowing its key.
The cadence at the end of a melody is what confirms its key.
A tonic arpeggio is the tonic triad played as a broken chord across octaves.
A broken tonic triad and a broken chord on any degree use the same hand shape and motion.
Finding a third and a fifth above a note is how a block triad is built at the keyboard.
Playing I - IV - V - I in a new key is transposing a progression at the keyboard.
Several orchestral instruments transpose, such as the clarinet in B flat and the horn in F.
An even scale needs even loudness from every finger as well as even timing.
Scales at exam tempo are played in even sixteenth notes against the beat.
Scales and pieces reach tempo the same way: steady at a slow speed, then stepped up.
Hands-together scales train both hands to land each note at the same moment.
Contrary-motion scales mirror the fingering in each hand, an easier first case of hands landing together.
A sight-reading routine starts by finding the key from the signature and the last note.
Voice leading is written for the four SATB voices, each moving as little as possible.
Broken chords and arpeggios are held together by the pedal through one harmony.
The pedal changes on each chord change, so pedalling a progression means hearing where the harmony moves.
An Alberti bass has to sit quietly under the melody it accompanies.
A mordent decorates a note with its upper or lower neighbour, the same shape as an auxiliary note.
An appoggiatura is a note outside the chord that leans onto a chord note, like an accented passing note.
A waltz bass plays out triple metre: the bass on one, the chord on two and three.
An Alberti bass is a steady left-hand rhythm in even quavers or semiquavers.
Passing notes usually fall between the beats, while chord notes fall on them.
An accompaniment pattern in a piece has to be played evenly so the melody can sit on it.
The Alberti bass is the classic pattern an even accompaniment is judged on.
Playing a melody over chords is the melody-and-accompaniment texture at the keyboard.
Phrases in a piece end on cadences, most clearly the perfect cadence at the end.
The first half of a binary piece often ends on an imperfect cadence, leaving the music open.
Memorising a piece by its harmony, knowing where tonic, predominant and dominant fall, holds up better than finger memory alone.
Following a piece's repeats and first and second endings relies on reading repeat signs.
D.C. and D.S. with Fine and Coda decide the order a piece is played in.
A piece's tempo marking is usually an Italian tempo term.
Shaping a phrase means knowing where it starts and the cadence it is heading to.
Melody over accompaniment only reads as that texture when the melody is louder than the accompaniment.
Building up to tempo ends at playing at the marked tempo.
An even accompaniment needs even loudness as well as even timing.
